points.name: BOMA covers commercial building operations

points.name: NAR REACH backs the startups

points.desc: The residential brokerage's platform applies AI to agent workflows, client matching, and predictive listing recommendations.
points.name: Compass runs AI inside the brokerage workflow

points.name: Smart buildings close the operations loop

summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
# Real Estate

According to the Census Bureau, 28.9 percent of real estate and rental and leasing firms reported using AI in the two weeks prior to their most recent survey, up from 28.0 percent in the prior period. This adoption sits largely in three workflows: property valuation, lease management, and building operations automation. The sector's maturity shows in the regulatory treatment of its primary AI application—automated valuation models, or AVMs—which determine collateral value in mortgage lending. The FHFA, CFPB, OCC, Board, FDIC, and NCUA have jointly mandated quality control standards for AVMs used by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers, requiring institutions to adopt policies and procedures that ensure high confidence in AVM estimates, protect against data manipulation, avoid conflicts of interest, and submit to random sample testing and reviews. This represents the first binding federal framework for production AI in the sector.

The valuation layer runs on published machine learning models deployed at scale. Zillow publishes Zestimates for 110 million homes using neural network architectures that incorporate county records, tax assessor data, and MLS feeds, with updated models designed to reduce error rates while improving responsiveness to local trends and seasonal shifts. HouseCanary delivers valuations and forecasts for over 136 million U.S. properties using AI-driven analytics and image recognition to assess property condition from photos. These platforms and others like Opendoor—whose pricing models carry direct balance-sheet exposure—form the consumer and institutional valuation infrastructure. Vendors compete on data breadth, model refresh frequency, and accuracy claims, though the sources do not quantify ROI metrics for end-users.

Commercial real estate operations deploy AI for lease abstraction, building management, and portfolio intelligence. Prophia uses AI to extract lease terms and combines them with expert validation to produce structured lease data for risk mitigation and decision-making. EliseAI applies agentic conversational AI to property management workflows, automating responses to leads, residents, and maintenance requests while integrating with existing systems. Building Engines' Prism platform, a JLL company, delivers recommendations and automation for end-to-end operations, helping teams cut costs and grow net operating income. These tools target operational efficiency and faster decision cycles rather than new revenue streams, yet the sources contain no reported savings or productivity benchmarks.

The residential brokerage side concentrates AI in client matching, tour automation, and listing analytics. Compass integrates AI into agent workflows and buyer-seller pairing. The National Association of Realtors operates REACH, a scale-up program for proptech vendors backed by Second Century Ventures, described as the most active venture fund in global real estate technology. CREtech hosts the commercial proptech industry's largest annual conference, drawing 3,000 leaders and facilitating 20,000 one-on-one meetings among owners, developers, brokers, and tech companies. CRETI tracks proptech capital flows as a research organization. These venues and funds indicate concentrated venture attention, though the sources do not break out capital figures or identify dominant vendors by funding or valuation.

Regulatory risk centers on AVM quality and bias. The federal AVM standards require policies addressing model accuracy, data integrity, and conflicts of interest—implicitly acknowledging past failures to catch valuation errors or discriminatory outcomes in mortgage lending. The CFPB's enforcement record and ongoing algorithmic-appraisal work remain the supervisory record of how valuation bias and model accountability are enforced in practice. Beyond AVMs, the sources reveal no other sectoral AI regulations or compliance frameworks. For firms evaluating deployment, the takeaway is that valuation AI now operates under binding federal scrutiny while operational AI remains largely unregulated, and published methodologies from Zillow and similar platforms offer rare transparency into production models, though adoption ROI remains undocumented in these sources.
